module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# The $\frac 1 3$–$\frac 2 3$ conjecture

*Reference:* [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1/3%E2%80%932/3_conjecture)
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Conjecture_1_3_to_2_3

/--
Does every finite partially ordered set that is not totally ordered
contain two elements $x$ and $y$ such that the probability that
$x$ appears before $y$ in a random linear extension is between $\frac 1 3$ and $\frac 2 3$?

The set of all total order extensions is represented as order preserving
bijections $P$ of $1, ..., n$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 6]
theorem conjecture_1_3_to_2_3 : answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ (P : Type) [Finite P] [PartialOrder P]
    (not_total : ¬ Std.Total (α := P) (· ≤ ·)) (total_ext : Set <| OrderHom P ℕ)
    (total_ext_def : ∀ σ, σ ∈ total_ext ↔ Set.range σ = Set.Icc 1 (Nat.card P)),
    ∃ x y : P, ({σ ∈ total_ext | σ x < σ y}.ncard / total_ext.ncard : ℚ)
      ∈ Set.Icc (1/3) (2/3) := by
  sorry

end Conjecture_1_3_to_2_3

reformulations.difference: Linear extensions are represented by monotone maps σ : P →o ℕ with range exactly Set.Icc 1 (Nat.card P). Bijectivity onto this interval is implicit rather than explicitly required.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For finite P of cardinality n, the interval {1,…,n} also has n elements. Surjectivity onto it therefore forces injectivity. Conversely, a bijection onto this interval has the required range. These monotone bijections correspond uniquely to linear extensions via their rank maps, preserving both the uniform counts and the event that x precedes y. In /workspace/review/scratch.lean, Review.range_iff_bijection proves the equivalence of the range condition with existence of such a bijection. The scratch file also proves that the extension set is finite and nonempty.

sources_consulted: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1/3%E2%80%932/3_conjecture — statement, examples, definitions, history, partial results, and related conjectures.
Imed Zaguia, “The 1/3–2/3 Conjecture for ordered sets whose cover graph is a forest,” arXiv:1610.00809, abstract and §1; LaTeX source read from https://arxiv.org/e-print/1610.00809.
review.notes: Checked the sole theorem, including answer scope and polarity, quantifiers, inclusive bounds, and boundary cases. The non-totality hypothesis excludes empty and singleton posets; equal x and y cannot satisfy the positive lower bound. Lean confirms that division is rational and that total_ext_def uniquely determines a set with positive cardinality. Computable finite-rank tests reproduce probability 1/2 for the two-element antichain and probabilities 1/3 and 2/3 for Wikipedia’s three-element example. The final scratch file compiles successfully. Wikipedia still records the general conjecture as unsolved, consistent with research open.
